The two men began to hear strange noises and they thought it was the work of the supernatural. They decided to leave and as they were walking in the forest one of them picked up a bone and the other took a stone. When they came across a clearing the man with the bone threw it to the ground and it turned into a mighty beast. The other man also threw his object to the ground and it turned into a mighty beast as well. The two beasts fought each other and the forest was shaken by their combat. When the battle was over, the two men picked up their objects and left. When they got to the village they told the other people of what had happened and then they all went back to their homes.

Analysis
The story is a good example of the transformation common in many Native American tales. The story also demonstrates the respect the Haidas had for nature. The animals were considered to be a part of the village and the people had to live in harmony with them.

A monstrous water creature appeared and grabbed one of them, throwing him into the air, and then another creature appeared and attacked the other man with its tail. Both men were killed and their bodies washed up on the shore near the village.

After this, the people of Egulac became very afraid and did not go out on the river any more. The chief of the village decided that something had to be done to protect the people from the creatures in the river, so he put a plan into action. He had a large wooden box made and placed bait inside. When the creatures came to take the bait, the box would be lowered into the water and then the trap would be sprung, trapping the creatures inside.

The plan worked and the creatures were trapped in the box. When the people of Egulac came to the shore they saw that the box was shaking and making strange noises, and they were very afraid. But the chief told them that it was only the creatures and they were trapped.

He then ordered the men to cut the box open, but when they did, the creatures changed into the forms of two old women. They explained that they were once good spirits who had been turned into monsters by the people of Kawaw. They asked the people of Egulac to forgive them and let them live among them. The chief agreed and the spirits lived among the people as healers and teachers.

The story of the water creatures is told by the Tlingit people of the Pacific Northwest.

While they were out seal hunting on the banks of the Bella Coola River, a thick fog came down and the young man became frightened. His father built a fire to keep away the cold and the young man begged to go home. But Tlako's Son was not satisfied with just a fire, he wanted a woman too. Tlako told his son to be quiet but a big raven came out of the fog and stood by the fire. The young man cried out in fear and the raven took him and flew away with him. Tlako searched for his son but could not find him. In the morning Tlako turned into a mountain and his son became a great rock at the entrance of the canyon.

In the story
The story of Tlako and his son is part of a larger story cycle that includes the Raven stories. The story is told in several versions, and the events are often rearranged. In one version, Tlako's Son is transformed into a raven and flies away. In another version, Tlako's Son is transformed into a woman and lives with the people. In some versions, Tlako is transformed into a mountain, and in others, he disappears from the story.

The tale
The story begins with two young men from Egulac going down to the river to hunt seals. It is night, and the sky is foggy and calm. Suddenly, a large sea monster appears and grabs one of the young men. The other young man runs back to the village to warn the people.
The people take up sticks and stones and go down to the water to drive away the monster. They find the monster's lair at the far side of an island. The monster is there with the young man and the woman whom it had taken. The people take the two young men and woman back to the village.
The monster gets angry and comes to the village to take revenge. The people take canoes and go out on the water to look for the monster. They find the monster's lair and the monster is there with the two young men and woman. The people take the two young men and woman away from the monster. The monster is angry and comes to the village a second time. The people are ready for it, and they kill the monster.

One young man was carried out to sea by the tide and the other young man saw this happening and went to the chief at Egulac. They had a council and they decided to go out and look for the missing young man.

The story is told by William W. Brown, a Haida of the Kaigani Haida people who lived at the time of the story in the early 1900s. He told the story to John R. Swanton, a Bureau of American Ethnology employee, in 1907.

In this story, the young man does not die, nor does he obtain an object, but he does return from a dangerous place. The other man, named Gusgus, suggested that they go closer to the water to see what was making the sounds. They left their boat and approached the water's edge. The people of the village were amazed to see Lhunana and asked him where he had been. Lhunana told them the story of how Gusgus had been taken by the serpent.
The people of Egulac were very upset about Gusgus' disappearance. They decided to conduct a search for Gusgus. They searched all day and all night but they could not find him. The people of Egulac were very upset and sad.
One day, while some of the men of Egulac were out hunting seals, they heard a loud roar. They turned around and saw the serpent. They shot at the serpent with their rifles, but the bullets did not harm the serpent. The serpent roared again and then it dove back into the water. The men of Egulac watched as the serpent swam away. They knew that they had killed Gusgus.
The people of Egulac were very upset. They held a big funeral for Gusgus. They made a big box and put Gusgus' body inside of it. They made a big mound and put the box inside of it. They held a feast in Gusgus' honor. The men of Egulac vowed that they would never go out to hunt seals again.

One young man was carried away by the river and drowned. The other young man went back to the village and told the people what had happened. The chief said they should go and get the body of their relative who had drowned. They went back to the place where he had drowned and they found the body of their relative hanging from a tree. The two young men were suddenly frightened, and as they cowered behind a rock they saw a canoe coming towards them.  It was manned by a single figure who was rowing with one hand while holding a glowing coal in the other hand.  The figure was the Loon Man.

The Loon Man was a supernatural being who was feared by the people of Egulac.  He was said to be the cause of all accidents on the water and could cause fog to come down at any time.  The Loon Man was also said to be able to transform himself into the shape of a loon and fly over the water.

The canoe drew closer and the Loon Man spoke to the two young men.  He asked them why they were out on the water at night and why they were afraid.  The young men stammered their excuses and apologies and the Loon Man then told them that they would not be harmed that night.  He then threw the glowing coal onto the shore and warned the young men never to be out on the water at night unless they had good reason and were warned by the elders.

The two young men returned to their village and warned the others of the encounter.  From then on the people of Egulac were more careful and only went out on the water at night if they had good reason and were warned by the elders.

The younger man was afraid and asked the elder to go home. But the elder wanted to continue hunting and went a little further out into the water. Suddenly a sea monster appeared and grabbed him. The younger man was terrified and ran back to the village, where he told the chief what had happened. The chief then went to the place where the elder had been taken, and he threw a rock into the water and made a prayer. Then he went back to the village and waited until morning. When the sun came up, the chief went out to the spot where the elder had been taken and found that a great stone had appeared there, and on the stone was written: "Egulac, the Seal Hunter, has been taken to the land of the spirits. He will return to you after three nights. Do not worry." And on the third night, Egulac returned.

The story
The story of Egulac is a Haida oral tradition, and is one of the few Haida tales that is known in more than one version. The version above is the most common one, but there is another version that is told by Charles Clouston. In this version, Egulac is not a seal hunter, but a "warrior and hunter". In this version, Egulac goes out to the lagoon to hunt sea otters, and not seals. When the sea monster takes Egulac, he is not taken to the land of the spirits, but to the "bottom of the sea". And in this version, Egulac is not brought back to life by a stone, but by a "magic breath" from the Raven.

Analysis
The story of Egulac is a creation myth, because it explains how a Haida hero became a spirit and how a stone came to be. It is also a transformation story, because the hero changes his form, first becoming a spirit and then returning to the world of the living. The story also has elements of a hero myth, because Egulac is a brave and strong hero who goes out to hunt in the darkness and is taken by a monster.

The story
Long ago, there was a village called Egulac. It was located where the village of Alert Bay is now. Two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals. It was a foggy and calm night. The two men were out in the canoe and they heard strange noises. They saw two glowing lights coming towards them. They realized that the ghosts were coming for them. The ghosts were the spirits of people who had died in the water and they were angry because the living were disturbing their water. The two men ran back to their village and told the story. The people of Egulac decided to never go down to the river at night again.

Influence
The story of the Ghosts of the River is a cautionary tale that was used to keep the people of the village from going into the water at night. It is a story that has been passed down from generation to generation. The story has influenced the culture of the Kwakwaka'wakw people.

Analysis
The story of "Killer of Men" is an example of a transformation myth, in which a monster is appeased and transformed into something less dangerous. The story also shows the influence of contact with European culture, in the form of the potlatch.
The story is also an example of a type of creation story in which the world is considered to be in a state of balance, which can be disturbed by monstrous beings from the sea. In this story, the balance is disturbed by a seal hunter who disturbs the creature's lair, and only by appeasing the creature with a potlatch can the balance be restored.

A great monster came out of the water. The young men saw it and were afraid. The monster reached out with its tail and knocked one of the young men into the water. The other young man ran away and went back to his people. The monster followed the young man back to Egulac and destroyed the village. The people of Egulac all ran away to hide. The monster went back to the water.

The young man went back to the place where he had left his companion and found that he had been killed by the monster. The young man cried for his companion. His cry went out over the water and reached his people. His people came back to the village and saw that it had been destroyed. They were very upset.
The young man held a funeral for his companion and then went to the place where his people had hidden. His people were very glad to see him and they all worked together to build a new village.
The young man went back to the place where he had killed the monster and cut off its head. He took the head back to his village and put it on a pole.
From then on the people of Egulac lived in peace.

The story
This story is from Tlingit tradition. It was recorded in 1880 by Father P. J. Sainz, a Catholic missionary. It was part of a "cycle of stories" told by members of the Raven clan of the Tlingit people. The story was told by "a young man named Charles of the Eagle moiety".

Analysis
This story is an example of a revenge myth. It is also an example of a hero myth. In this myth, the hero is a young man who goes out and performs a brave deed. The young man in this story is also an avenger. He avenges the death of his companion and protects his people by killing the monster that destroyed their village.
The monster in this story is a sea monster. Sea monsters are common in Native American mythology.

Analysis
This story is an example of a revenge tale, where the creature from the story gets revenge on the two men for disbelieving his story. The story is also an example of a transformation story where the creature transforms from a bear to a raven and back to a bear and then to a human and finally to a storyteller. The story is also an example of a tale where the supernatural punishes humans for their disbelief. Egulac was a village on the northwest coast of Vancouver Island, about 20 miles west of the present site of Port Alberni. It was the home of the people called the Tsesis, who were a branch of the Hupa. The name Tsesis means "people of the sea." They lived by fishing and hunting seals.

The body of the serpent was 120 feet long and 30 feet around. The head and tail were carried to a high place, and the rest of the body was buried in a deep pit. The people of Egulac celebrated for many days.

The head and tail of the serpent were made into rattles and worn by the war leaders in battle.

The story of the killing of the serpent was told by the Hupa people for many generations. It was first written down by Thomas G. Lowe in 1907.

The story
This story was told by a Tlingit named Charles "Charlie" Ediz Hook, who was born in 1928. It comes from the Tlingit people, who lived in what is now Sitka, Alaska. The story was passed down through oral tradition, and was told to Charlie by his father.

Analysis
The story has several elements common to Native American folklore. These include the presence of a supernatural being that can only be seen in certain conditions, in this case at night and near water. The story also includes a moral, in this case that people should be careful at night and avoid taking unnecessary risks.

Interpretation
The story "The Night Before" is a narrative of a prophecy in the oral tradition of the Haida people. The story relates a warning of the impending destruction of a Haida village by a volcanic eruption, and the subsequent relocation of the village to a new location on the Haida Gwaii archipelago. The story was recorded in 1907 by Edward W. Nelson, a Canadian Indian agent, from the testimony of a Haida elder named Charles Clow. According to Nelson, Clow was "a chief of the Eagle tribe of the Haida tribe".

Analysis
"The Night Before" is an example of a "volcano story", a genre of myths recorded among many indigenous North American populations. These stories relate a warning of a coming catastrophe, usually a volcanic eruption, and the relocation of a tribe to a new location. The genre is found among many indigenous populations of the Pacific Northwest, including the Haida, Tlingit, Kwakiutl, Bella Coola, and Okanagan. The precise meaning of these stories varies among different tribes, but generally they relate a warning of an impending volcanic eruption, and a prophecy that the tribe must relocate to a new location to avoid destruction. The story

Analysis
The story of Star Husband is one of many stories told by the Tlingit people that explain why things are the way they are. It is a story that shows the power of the natural world and the power of the stars. It also shows the relationship between the natural world and the Tlingit people. Another story that is told by the Tlingit people is the story of Raven Steals the Light, which is also told by other Northwest Coast groups.

After a few days, the people of Egulac decided to conduct a ceremony to appease the sea monster and prevent further attacks. A young woman named K'adhi was chosen to be the ceremonial leader and was given new clothes and a new name, Tsonakwa. She was then taken to the river's edge and left alone. The sea monster appeared and carried her off to the east, leaving her on an island. The ceremony was repeated the following year, with a young man named K'ushtaka chosen to be the ceremonial leader. He was given the name Tsonakwa and taken to the river's edge. The sea monster appeared and carried him off to the west, leaving him on an island with Tsonakwa. The two young people were terrified and afraid, but after some time they began to explore the island. They found that the island was rich in food and resources and began to build a village. After a few years they decided to return to their people. Tsonakwa and K'ushtaka returned to their people and told them of their experiences. The people were amazed and impressed, and from that day on the Tsonakwa ceremony was conducted every year to appease the sea monster and ensure the continued prosperity of the village.

In later years, the Tsonakwa ceremony was conducted by a hereditary chief. The first hereditary chief was K'ushtaka's son, whose name was also K'ushtaka. The chiefs were also called "Seal Bringers" because they were believed to have a special power to bring seals to the village.

In the story, Egulac refers to a mythical place where the people of the tribe lived. It is likely that the storyteller confused the name of the tribe with the name of the place where they lived.

The story is part of the collection of James Mooney, a Bureau of American Ethnology agent who recorded Native American folklore.

The younger man was afraid and asked the older man to go home, but the older man said they should wait until morning. In the morning they went home and the younger man told his chief that they had been attacked by a sea monster and that his companion was dead. The chief then ordered that the younger man be put to death, because he was afraid that the tribe would become too weak to hunt if they lost one of its members. The older man was put on a scaffold and the younger man was put to death. After the younger man's death, the older man was put to death also, even though he had told the truth.

Variants
There are many variants of this story. In some versions, the two men are not from Egulac but from different tribes. In some versions, the younger man is put to death for disobeying the chief's orders.

Media
The story has inspired several works of fiction. Clara Downey's 1913 novel The Eagle Shield retells the story, setting it in 1880 and making the two men members of different clans of the Tlingit tribe. The 1920 silent film The Seal Skinner is based on the story, with the two men being members of different Eskimo tribes. The story is also the basis of the 1951 short story "The Seal Men" by Robert Bloch. The 1958 short story "The Fog" by Ray Bradbury is a retelling of the story set in the fictional town of Samhain on the coast of Oregon. The 1981 short story "The Fog at the Edge of the World" by Jane Yolen is a retelling of the story set among the Inuit. The 1994 short story "The Seal Hunter's Tale" by Peter Behrens is a retelling of the story set among the Haida. The 2008 short story "The Tale of the Fog" by Donna J. McMorris is a retelling of the story set among the Tsimshian. The 2012 short story "The Fog" by Brian Evanson is a retelling of the story set among the Yupik.

The story
The story of the sea monster comes from the Tlingit people of the Pacific Northwest. It was told by Charles C. Hill, a Tlingit from Sitka, to James Mooney, a collector for the Bureau of American Ethnology in 1890. It is a version of the Raven Cycle, a collection of stories about the trickster Raven.

Analysis
The story of the sea monster is one of many tales in which a sea monster is lured out of the water and killed. The story shares similarities with the story of the Loch Ness monster Ingelheim Dragon, and the Beast of Gevaudan. The story also shares similarities to the story of the killer whale that killed a man in the waters of Lituya Bay, near Chatham, New Jersey in 1979.

The Windigo chased the villagers into the woods, where it began to destroy the huts. The Windigo then began to hunt the people of the village. The only one who was able to escape was an old woman, who had been away picking berries. She ran to a fortified camp on the other side of the lake and warned them of what had happened. The people of that village armed themselves and went back to Egulac to fight the Windigo.
They set a trap for the Windigo using a large log. When the Windigo came, they rolled the log onto it, pinning it. The Windigo was unable to free itself, and the villagers cut off its head. The Windigo's body was burned up, but its head was kept as a reminder of what had happened.

The two men began to hear strange noises and saw two glowing red eyes. The eyes were attached to a large creature which was standing on two legs. The creature began to chase the two men and they ran back to their village. The elder of the two men took a piece of bone and drew a picture of the creature in the sand. The next morning the villagers saw the picture and knew what had visited them. The creature came back many nights and the villagers tried many things to scare it away. They made loud noises, set fires, and set traps but nothing seemed to work. One night the creature took a young girl. The villagers decided they had to kill the creature. They set up a trap and when the creature came they threw rocks at it and hit it with sticks. The creature roared, let out a loud scream and disappeared. The villagers never saw the creature again but they always remembered the creature that came to their village that night.

Analysis
The story of the Egulac Giant is a typical example of a creature story told by the Heiltsuk people of the Central Coast of British Columbia. It is similar to the stories of the Wind Woman, the Sea Serpent, and the Thunderbird. The creature is described as being very tall, having glowing red eyes, and making roaring and screaming noises. These are all common characteristics of monsters in the folklore of many cultures. The creature is also described as being very powerful. It is able to chase two young men, run as fast as them, and jump high enough to clear a large tree. It is also able to scare the villagers with its roars and screams. The creature is also very intelligent, as it was able to understand drawings. The reason why the creature was in the village is not clear, as the story does not give an explanation for its actions. It is possible that the creature was just looking for food, as it was by the river hunting for seals. Another possibility is that the creature was just curious about the villagers. The story of the Egulac Giant is a good example of a cautionary tale, as the villagers were able to protect themselves from the creature by using their knowledge and working together.

Influence
The story of "Egulac" is believed to be the basis for the story of the Headless Man in Edgar Allan Poe's short story "The Tell-Tale Heart". The story was first published in 1839, eight years before Poe moved to New York and ten years before he moved to Philadelphia, where he was said to have gotten the idea for the story from a local legend. The character of the Headless Man is similar to the ghost in "Egulac", in that they both have white eyes and tell the protagonist that they are going to kill them. In both stories, the ghosts are able to appear in the real world and can move around when no one is looking. In both stories, the ghosts are able to make noises that make the protagonists go mad and cause them to confess to their crimes.

The younger man was afraid and asked the older man to take him home, but the older man said he couldn't because he had left his gun on the other side of the river and he was going back to get it. The younger man insisted on going home, and after much pleading the older man agreed to take him across the river. As they were crossing, however, a big wave came and knocked the older man off of his feet, and he was swept away by the current and disappeared. The younger man was very upset, and after a few days he decided to go out and hunt seals to avenge his friend's death. He hunted and hunted but did not find any seals, and after a long time he became very tired and lay down on a rock to rest. While he was sleeping, his friend appeared to him in a dream and told him that he had not been killed by the wave, but had been changed into a seal by the chief of the river because of his great love for the sea. The younger man was very happy to hear this, and from then on he never killed any sea creatures.

Analysis
The story of "The Seal People" is an example of a transformation story, a common motif in Native American folklore. In this story, the Egulac youth undergoes a physical transformation as well as a rite of passage, changing him into an older, wiser man. It is also an example of a revenge story, in which the protagonist sets out to avenge the death of a loved one. The story also contains themes of friendship and the supernatural.

Structural analysis
The story of "The Seal People" follows a standard folktale structure. It begins with an introduction of the setting and the two main characters. The first complication is introduced when the younger man becomes afraid and wants to go home. The first crisis occurs when the older man disappears. The second complication is the younger man's desire for revenge. The second crisis is when the younger man falls asleep and his friend leaves him. The third complication is the younger man's inability to find food, and the fourth crisis is when the younger man sees his friend as a seal. The story concludes with the resolution of the younger man seeing his friend as a seal and realizing that he must not kill them.

They heard a noise behind them and turned to see a monster rising out of the water. They ran as fast as they could but the monster was too fast and soon caught them. The monster threw them both into the water and they were drowned. The monster then went back into the water.

Analysis
This story comes from Tlingit tradition and is a common tale among the Tlingit people. It is a cautionary tale about going out at night, especially during foggy or calm weather, as during these times the monsters that live in the water will come out to hunt.

Variants
This story is also known as "The Man-Dog".
Another version of this story is known as "The Girl Who Married a Monster". In this version a girl marries a monster and has two children with him before realizing that he is a monster and leaving him. One night while she is out alone the monster comes out and kills her.

The Girl Who Married a Monster was filmed by the Smithsonian Institution in 1970.

One young man said to the other: "I am going to take advantage of this fog to sneak up on the seal herd and attack them. You stay here and keep watch over our camp and our equipment." His companion agreed.
The first young man hunted so successfully that he brought home a great many seal skins. His friend, however, had been careless and had fallen asleep. When he awoke, he discovered that his companion was missing. He searched for him but to no avail.
Finally he returned to their camp and an old man was there waiting for him. The old man said, "I am the spirit of this place. Your friend has been taken by the seal people and will never return. You have hunted the seals without my permission, so now I will take something from you." The old man took the young man's eyesight.
When the young man returned to his village, his people were amazed to see him without his eyesight, for he had been gone only a short time. They were also amazed that he had brought home a great many seal skins.
Later, in a dream, the young man learned that his companion was living with the seal people, who had given him the gift of perfect darkness so he could hunt in the deep water where the seals slept.

Suddenly a great light appeared and an enormous voice spoke to them. The voice came from the waters and it was the Great Spirit telling them that he was going to give them a great gift. He told them he would give them a secret that would be a great help to them.

The story of how the Great Spirit gave Loon and Otter the power to call on the loon and the otter for help is a story that has been passed down from generation to generation among the Ojibway people. The monster followed them and when it was about to attack, a chief appeared and saved them. The chief was so impressed that he took the two men back to his village and made them warriors.

This is a tale of the Haida people, told by Charles Hill-Tout in 1916.

Variants
This story is told by John A. Mikkines in 1975, with slight variations.

The tale
Two Haida boys were out on the beach one night hunting seals. It was a foggy, still night. One said he heard something moving in the water, the other didn't believe him. They argued about it until suddenly a sea monster rose out of the water. The two boys ran away as fast as they could. The monster followed them, but just as it was about to catch them, the chief appeared out of nowhere and chased the monster away. He was so impressed with the boys that he took them back to his village and made them warriors.

Analysis
This tale is a good example of a "monster-as-helper" story. In this story, the monster is not evil, but rather acts as a guardian of the village. The story also shows the importance of the chief in Haida culture. He is the only one who can control the monster, and he is the one who decides the fate of the boys.

Analysis
The story of the Egulac monster is similar to the story of the Loch Ness Monster, a creature that is said to inhabit the waters of Loch Ness in Scotland. The creature in this story is also similar to the Thunderbird, a creature from Native American mythology. The creature in this story is described as being very large, having a red mouth and a smell like burnt tar, which is similar to the descriptions of the Loch Ness Monster. The creature in this story is also described as having a glowing light, which could be a reference to the bioluminescence that some animals have. The creature in this story disappears when it is seen directly, which is similar to the creature in the story of the Lake Champlain Monster. The story of the Egulac monster may have been influenced by contact with Scottish settlers, who would have told stories of the Loch Ness Monster. It is also possible that the story of the Egulac monster is a modern legend that was invented to explain the unexplained.

One day he decided that he wanted to give a feast for all of his people. He killed many seals and salmon and prepared a great feast. After the feast he gave away all of his extra things to the poor. After that he was just as rich as before but now he was also popular.
After the feast Heeka-Weyi wanted more. He wanted to have the largest potlatch that the world had ever seen. He worked for months preparing for the potlatch. He killed more seals and salmon than he ever had before. He gave away all of his extra things to the poor again.
When the day of the potlatch came everyone in the village came. There was food and games and everything that you could ever want. Everyone was having fun.
When the fun was over Heeka-Weyi gave away all of his clothes and blankets and tools. He gave away his beautiful house. He gave away everything that he owned.
After the potlatch Heeka-Weyi was poor. He was poorer than anyone in the village. But he didn't care. He was happy because he knew that he had given the best potlatch that anyone had ever had.
That night Heeka-Weyi and his family slept outside in the open because all of their blankets and bedding was gone. In the middle of the night Heeka-Weyi woke up and looked up at the stars. He said to himself "I am a poor man." He fell asleep thinking that.
In the morning when Heeka-Weyi woke up he was rich again. All of his things were back.

They heard a noise behind them and when they looked back, saw a canoe with two men in it coming towards them. The two young men from Egulac reached for their guns and shot both of the men in the canoe. After they had killed these two men, they took their bodies to the village of Esquimalt, where they reported the incident to the chief.
The chief took the bodies and buried them and then sent messengers to all the nearby villages to warn them of the arrival of the ghosts of the two men from the sea. He also forbade any hunting until the hunters had made offerings to the dead men's spirits.
After some time had passed, two young men from Esquimalt went out hunting and as they were returning home in their canoe they saw a canoe with two men in it approaching them. The two men in the second canoe asked the hunters to give them a ride as their canoe had been swamped in a rapid. The hunters agreed and the four men rowed to the shore together.
As they were walking through the village, the two ghosts told the living men that they had been killed unjustly and that the men who had killed them would die in war. They also told the living men that the village would be destroyed and that only the man who killed the chief would survive.
After the ghosts had left the living men, they went to the chief and told him all that had happened. The chief said that they had been warned not to hunt until they had made offerings to the dead men's spirits, but they had not listened. He then told the hunters that they would be going to war and that they would be killed.
A few days later, two young men from the village went out hunting and while they were out in their canoe they were attacked by a war party from a nearby village. The two hunters were killed and their bodies were brought back to the village.
A few days later, two young men from the village went out sealing and as they were returning home in their canoe they were attacked by a war party from a nearby village. The men in the canoe were killed and their bodies were brought back to the village.

A monster appeared and attacked them. The young men ran back to their village and warned the people. The chief decided that two young men should go out every night to see if the monster is still there.

One night, when the two young men were out on the beach hunting seals, the monster came to the shore. The monster was so big that it cast a shadow over the whole village. The monster had a long neck and a long tail, and it breathed fire. The two young men grabbed their clubs and ran away as fast as they could.

The monster followed them and they ran into the long house. The people of the village came out to fight the monster. They threw spears and stones at the monster but they didn't hurt it. The monster just breathed fire at the long house.

The chief decided that they should try to scare the monster away. So they gathered many torches and set them on fire. When the monster came back, they all ran out of the long house and threw the torches at the monster. The monster roared and ran away.

The next day the monster was gone and it never came back. The Haida people believed that the monster had gone back to the sea and would never come back.

Song
This is the song that the Haida sing about the monster:

Long time ago, by the water,
Two young men out hunting for food,
Suddenly came a noise,
A monster by the shore.
Monster by the shore.

Long neck, long tail,
Breathes fire, hot and pale,
Run, run, run,
Into the long house,
Safe, safe, safe.
Monster by the shore.

Torches, bright and red,
Chief by my side,
Brave warriors all,
Stand up tall,
Scare away,
Monster far,
Monster gone,
Never to come back,
Monster by the shore.

Variants
This story is told by many Northwest Coast tribes, with variations including the names of the characters and the outcome of the story. 
A version told by the Tlingit people of Southeast Alaska has the older man's head being taken by the monster as a trophy. In this version the younger man is named Gyaalx'áat and the older man is named Aa. 
A version told by the Heiltsuk people of British Columbia has the younger man's name as Xaaym and the older man's name as Xaak'u. In this version the monster is named Xeex'a and is described as being a sea otter. In this version the older man escapes by disguising himself as a seaweed. 
A version told by the Nisga'a people of British Columbia has the younger man's name as Xiikw'a and the older man's name as Xiis. In this version the monster is named Ligaat and is described as being a giant sea lion. In this version the older man escapes by jumping onto a protruding log. 
A version told by the Haida people of British Columbia has the younger man's name as Xiikw'a and the older man's name as Xiis. In this version the monster is named Kusp'u and is described as being a giant octopus. In this version the older man escapes by climbing a tree.

The story was adapted into the 1998 animated short film Xaaym and Aa, by Bill Reeves and Dean Steadman, for the National Film Board of Canada.

They heard a voice singing. It was a beautiful voice, clear and musical, and the two young men were enchanted by it. They searched around in the fog for the source of the voice, but they could not find it.

Suddenly a great light appeared and a woman stepped out of it. She was dressed in white robes and her hair was dark. She was standing on the shore of the river with one foot, and she was holding a small child in her arms. The young men were very afraid when they saw her.

The woman said to them, "Do not be afraid. I am the Spirit of the Water. I have been singing to comfort the children in the canoes. I have come to take this child to the other side. I will leave him with your people. You must take care of him."

Then the woman gave the child to one of the young men and she disappeared with the other young man. The young man who held the child looked at it and it was a beautiful baby boy.

The young man took the baby to his village and he and his people took good care of the child. And the child grew up strong and healthy and happy. And when he grew up he became a great chief and his people loved him.

And the people said that he was the child of the Spirit of the Water and they were proud of him.

Suddenly they heard a noise and saw a canoe coming towards them.  They drew their knives and ready to attack they saw a woman in the canoe.  She said "Do not be afraid I am not a ghost."  She introduced herself as Kliluk, the Sea-Hazel.  She told them that she had been watching them and wanted to see what they would do.  She then told them that she was a half human, half seal creature.  She went on to tell them that there was a great famine on land and that she could take them to the underwater land where they could find food.  The two young men agreed to go with her.  She took them to an underwater cave where they found a beautiful underwater world.  She warned them that they could not stay there forever and that they would have to leave when the time was right.  She gave them salmon and seal meat and told them to eat the last piece of meat when they had to leave.  When they left the underwater world they found that it was daylight and that they had been gone for many days.  They went back to their village and told the people about the underwater world.  The people did not believe them and thought that they were crazy.  The two young men found a place to live by themselves and they lived off the food that Kliluk had given them.  Eventually they ate the last piece of meat and from that time on they had to find their own food.  They became great hunters and were able to provide food for themselves and the people of their village.

Comparative mythology
This story is similar to the Greek myth of the Sirens, who lured sailors to shipwreck on the rocky coast of their island with their beautiful singing.

Interpretation
The story of the two young men from Egulac is an example of a Canadian folktale that describes encounters with supernatural beings. The story includes the idea of a trickster who takes the form of a man with one leg. The story also includes the idea of a canoe, which is a common object in many traditional Canadian tales. The story also includes the idea of a spirit from the underworld. The story also includes the idea of a man cutting people in half. This story is an example of a North American Indian legend.

A monstrous creature appeared and both young men were thrown into the water.  Only one of them managed to get out and he went back to Egulac and warned the people of what had happened.  The chief of the tribe decided to go down to the river with his best young men to hunt the creature and bring vengeance upon it.  They set traps all along the shore, and as the creature came out of the water it stepped on a trap and was captured.  The creature was described as being 20 feet long, 10 feet wide, and had the strength of ten men.  The creature was taken to Egulac and put on display.  The chief decided that the creature was too dangerous to be let free and ordered that it be killed.  The creature was burned and its ashes were scattered to the four winds.  After this the tribe began to decay and become filled with fighting and jealousy.  The story of the creature was told for generations to remind the tribe of the dangers of the world and the need to stick together.

In popular culture
The story of the Windigo has been retold many times, most notably in the 1930 short story "The Windigo" by Richard Adams and in the 1957 story "The Beast from the Sea" by Charles L. Harness, which was reprinted in his 1964 collection The Boundaries of Time. It was also referenced in Stephen King's novel It, and in the 1987 film Hellraiser. The 1988 film The Monster and the Magician was loosely based on the story. The 2004 video game Silent Hill 4: The Room features a creature based on the Windigo. The 2010 video game Dead Space 2 features a monster based on the Windigo, which is one of the bosses in the game. The 2014 video game Alien: Isolation features a creature based on the Windigo in one of the game's endings.

The two young men began to argue about who would get the canoe.  They stopped arguing briefly when they heard a story told by their great-grandfather, but began arguing again.  Suddenly, one of the young men grabbed a stick and struck the other on the head, causing him to fall into the water. At the end of the story, the chief decided that the young man who had been killed had been taken to the land of the dead and that he would come back to the world of the living as a great chief. Analysis
This story is an example of a revenge story, and also has elements of a murder story.  The story also has a prophecy that comes true.  There is also a hint of a love story, as the two young men were described as being like brothers.  The story also illustrates the importance of sharing and cooperation.  The story is also an example of a punishment story, as the one who caused the death was punished by being thrown out of the village.

Variants
A similar story is told about the village of Alert Bay, but instead of seals, salmon are being hunted. The story is also told about the village of Kingcome Inlet, but instead of seals, eagles are being hunted.

The story also has elements of a creation myth, as the woman is said to have created the first humans.

Analysis
The story of the chief and the river is a common one in many Northwest Coast cultures. The story has a clear moral, and the events in the story are meant to remind the listeners of the story to be careful and not to be arrogant.

The chief in the story is a classic trickster figure, in that he is arrogant and overconfident, and this overconfidence leads to his death. However, unlike the coyote or raven who are tricksters in many other Native American stories, the chief is not clever or funny. He is simply overconfident and arrogant.
The river in the story is also a powerful force, and is able to carry away the chief, despite his high rank. The river is able to punish the chief for his arrogance, and is able to make the chief learn humility, even after the chief's death.

I will take you to my island.  I will keep you there for as long as I want.  You will be my slaves.  You will do my work.  You will give me your bodies.  You will give me your strength.  When I am satisfied, I may let you go.  But perhaps I will keep you forever."  The two young men looked at each other.  They were afraid.  But they were also excited.  They were excited because they were young and strong and healthy.  They were excited because they were going to be slaves to the Spirit of the River.  They were excited because they were going to have wealth.  They clambered into the canoe and the Spirit of the River took them to her island.

The Spirit of the River kept the two young men slaves for a long, long time.  She made them do many things.  She made them dive under water and bring up heavy stones.  She made them cut wood and carry it to the other side of the island.  She made them row her canoe.  She made them do many sexual things.  After a long, long time she said to them, "You have served me well.  You have served me faithfully.  You have served me with strength and energy.  Now you may go."  The two young men left the island.  They went back to their village.  They were rich.  They were very strong.  They were famous.  They were proud.

The younger man heard a noise and looked over the side of the canoe and saw a sea monster. He told his companion, who did not believe him. The monster then grabbed the canoe and overturned it, putting the younger man on its back and carrying him a short distance before throwing him and the canoe onto the shore. The man ran away and reported what had happened to the elders of Egulac.
The elders sent for the older man who had not gone down to the river to hunt seals. He went down to the shore and saw the footprints of the creature in the sand. He followed the tracks until he came to a cave. He entered the cave and saw the creature lying on the ground. He crept up to it and threw a spear at it, killing it.
The elders held a ceremony to thank the gods for the successful hunt. They made a dance and sang a song that was sung for many generations.

Source
This story is from the book "Tales of the Bella Coola Indians" by James G. Swan, published in 1912. The story was told to Swan by a Bella Coola Indian named John Hunter.

In the beginning there was only darkness. The sun, the moon, and the stars did not yet shine. Only the great Creator Spirit lived in the land of light. But the Creator Spirit longed to share his light with the world.
So he called Raven, the great trickster, and said to him, "Raven, I want you to go down into the land of darkness and bring back some light for the people."
Raven flew down into the dark land and searched for light. He searched in caves and under waterfalls, but he found no light. Then he flew to the bottom of the great ocean and saw that it was dark there too. But in the deepest part of the ocean he saw a box made of solid light. In the box was a light so great that it could light up the whole world.
Raven took the light and flew back to the land of light and gave the light to the Creator Spirit. The Creator Spirit was very pleased and said, "Raven, you have done well. Now go and place the light where it will do the most good."
Raven flew all over the world and placed the light in the heads of the people. This is why people have the light of understanding between their eyebrows. And that is how Raven brought light to the world.

One young man, whose name was Kisal, began to walk ahead of the other. As he walked he began to hear a noise like the beating of a drum. The noise grew louder and closer. Suddenly, out of the fog came a monstrous whale that had been trapped by the tide in a shallow pool. Kisal tried to run back to his friend but he was too slow and the whale reached out with its tail and knocked him into the water. The whale then turned its attention to the other young man. Just as it was about to strike, Kisal's friend dived under its belly and held on tight. The whale then thrashed about in the water trying to shake the young man off. Kisal, who was still treading water, began to sing an old song that his grandmother had taught him. The song was about the whale's great-great-grandfather and how he once saved a drowning man. The whale stopped thrashing about and slowly raised its body out of the water. The young man clung to its smooth, slippery skin. When it was high enough, he climbed onto its back and onto the shore. The whale thrashed about in the water once more trying to knock the young man off but he held on tight and when it had finally given up he climbed down and walked away. Kisal was not so lucky. The whale had turned its attention back to him and it knocked him from its back and flung him high into the air with its tail. It was then that Kisal's friend heard the sound of a canoe approaching and soon after the whale disappeared back into the fog. When the canoe reached the spot where Kisal had been, it was empty.

Analysis
The story of the Whale is a tale of courage and the power of song. It is also a tragic story of loss. The story is similar to other tales in which a hero uses music to calm a wild beast. The story is also similar to the Inuit tale of the Killer Whale and the Boy.

Variants
There are many variants of this tale. In one version, the hero is a young woman named Kasaal. In another, the creature is a sea monster rather than a whale.

The story is an example of a creature that appears in many Indigenous folklore stories around the world, including the Thunderbird and Killer whale.

The tale is also an example of a "monster that kills" story, which have the following characteristics:

The monster is supernatural, and therefore is not subject to the laws of nature.
The monster is usually a solitary creature.
The monster attacks without provocation.
The monster is destructive, and kills for no reason other than it is a killer.
The monster is invulnerable to normal weapons and often to magical weapons as well.
The monster is indestructible.
The monster is immortal.
The monster is able to disguise itself as something other than a monster.
The monster is not a part of the natural world; it is a creature that has come from outside the normal world or one that has been cast out of the normal world.
The monster is a cannibal.
The monster is able to control the weather.
The monster is able to move great distances in a short time.The story is also an example of a "monster that helps" story, which have the following characteristics:

The monster is supernatural, and therefore is not subject to the laws of nature.

The monster helps the hero(es) in the story.
The monster gives the hero(es) a gift.

The story of the Canoe Man is a traditional story of the Tlingit people, told by the raven Na-Gee-Sha-Ka (Storyteller). The story is a cautionary tale, warning people not to go out at night when they should be asleep.

Analysis
The story of the Canoe Man is a traditional Tlingit story, passed down through generations of Tlingit people. It is a cautionary tale warning people, especially young people, to not go out at night when they should be asleep. The story also shows the Tlingit's belief in supernatural beings and the importance of their culture and traditions.

The younger man was afraid and asked the older man to go home, but the older man refused. Suddenly, a monster appeared in the water and snatched the younger man up in its jaws. The older man tried to save his companion but was unsuccessful and was also consumed by the monster.

Analysis
This story is an example of the Thunderbird cycle of stories, which is widespread among North American Indians. The story involves a flood, a common motif in many cultures. The story also has elements of a creation myth, as the monster in the story is said to have created the world.

Variants
This story is known in many variations, and is widespread among the tribes of the Pacific Northwest. It is also known among the tribes of the Plateau region. The story is also known on the northern Great Plains among the tribes such as the Assiniboine, Gros Ventre, and Blackfoot.
A variant of the story is told by the Haida, who call the transformer-hero Oo-kwus (or Ook-wus). In this version, the monster is a giant octopus rather than a whale.

The Wind-Handler's Son
Later the Wind-Handler's son fell in love with a frog. His father disapproved and refused to give his blessing, so the young man left his home and went to live with the frog-woman on an island near the mainland. There he remained for a long time, and his father eventually died.

Analysis
The story of "The Two Young Men from Egulac" is a good example of the way in which Eskimo stories often revolve around the themes of the supernatural and the spirit world. The story of Handsome Lake is part of the creation story of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) people. The story tells how the Great Spirit created the world and the people. The story says that the Great Spirit gave the people four sacred gifts: the Longhouse, the Constitution, the Prophecy and the Medicine. The story says that these gifts are sacred and that they must be kept pure and that if they are kept pure then the world will be kept in balance.

Variations
There are other variations of this tale. In some versions, the two young men are out hunting seals and are caught in a fog. While they are there, a group of spirits in blue and white appear and begin to surround them. The spirits are the ghosts of children who died in a smallpox epidemic. In this version, the spirits tell the young men that they will be protected as long as they remain on the beach until dawn. However, if they look back at the spirits, they will be turned into stones. The young men do as they are told and are saved. In other versions, the young men are out in a canoe when the fog comes in and the spirits appear. In this version, the spirits tell the young men that they will be protected as long as they do not speak. If they speak, they will be turned into stones. The young men do not speak and are saved.

Inspiration
The story is said to have inspired the name of the town of Alert Bay, as the first settlers thought that the spirits were a warning about the impending arrival of the Spanish.

Context
The story of Egulac is a Canadian folktale. The tale is of the Okanagan people, a First Nations group who lived in the Okanagan Valley in British Columbia, Canada. The story is a creation myth, explaining the origins of the people and their connection to the land.

Analysis
The story of Egulac is an example of a "feast culture" myth. These myths are common among Native American groups and often involve the ancestors of a group having a feast with the supernatural beings who created them. In these myths, the supernatural beings are often referred to as the "Food Givers." The creation of the food supply is often accompanied by the creation of the first people. In the story of Egulac, the people are created by the spirits and then are given food by them.
The story of Egulac also exhibits the idea of the "Dreamtime". In this story, the people have a dream in which they receive food and then they wake up and the food is there. This is a common theme in Native American mythology.

The two young men went to a mountain to be alone and there they saw the monster again. The monster spoke to them of many things and told them that he was the Giver of Life, the Creator. The young men asked the Creator what he would like them to do. The Creator told them to go back to their village and teach the people of their great power, and that they should use it for good.

The story of the Raven is a creation myth of the Haida people, told by a Haida named Charles Edenshaw. It was recorded by Franz Boas in the early 20th century.

The two men were Handsome Lake and his friend. Handsome Lake heard a voice calling out, "Bring me your fresh meat offerings." Handsome Lake threw a seal towards the voice but heard the voice again, "No, bring me your own flesh." Handsome Lake cut his own flesh and threw it towards the voice, then he heard the voice again, "I am the Great Spirit, hear me! I have made a covenant with you. You shall be the leader of your people. Your people will hunt their food as they have always done, but they shall no longer kill each other for sport or for women. You shall be their leader until the end of time." Handsome Lake then saw a vision of the Great Spirit and from then on was known as Tahamet or Father.

Variations
This story is also known as "The Coming of the Great Spirit to Handsome Lake".

They heard a voice singing, then another voice joined in and then a third. They thought, "This is strange, there are no people around here." They looked around but couldn't see anyone. Suddenly a great light appeared and in the midst of the light was the Raven.
The Raven spoke to them: "I have been watching you young men of Egulac. Your hearts are not pure. Go back to your people and tell them to live as they should. I will help you."
The two young men went back to their people and told them of the Raven's words. Their people were amazed and asked, "How could you see the Raven and live?"
From that time on the people of Egulac lived as they should and the Raven was pleased.

One young man was carried off by the water and was never seen again. The other young man went back to Egulac and told the people what had happened. The people decided to move to a different place. They moved to a place on the mainland where there was a salmon stream. The people had to travel a long distance to get to Egulac. They didn't like this so they moved back to the island.

The people of Egulac then decided to build a fortress on top of a hill so they could see any dangers coming. They also built a house for the chief. The chief's house was a long house that was 100 feet long and 30 feet high. The house had doors, windows, and a smoke hole. Inside the house there were beds, boxes, and shelves. There were also many people who lived in the house.

The people of Egulac also made tools, weapons, and fishing gear out of stone. They made spear points, scrapers, knives, and clubs out of stone. They made nets out of fish gut and bone. They made baskets out of cedar bark. The people of Egulac were very good at making things out of stone.

The people of Egulac were also good hunters. They hunted seal, sea lion, otter, bear, and deer. They used many different weapons to hunt. They used hooks, spears, clubs, nets, and traps. The people of Egulac also fished for salmon.

The people of Egulac had a big problem. They had no place to get fresh water. They had to get all of their water from the rain. The people of Egulac decided to build a water conduit. They made a long trench in the ground and put water in it. They put poles in the water to hold up a platform. They put another pole in the middle of the platform. They put a bucket on the top of the pole. When it rained they would go up to the bucket and get the water.

They heard a voice crying. They went to see what it was and they saw a woman with a light. The woman said to them, "I'm lost. You have to take me across the river and bring me to the other side."

So they took her across the river and when they got to the other side she disappeared. When the men looked back across the river they saw two stars where she had been standing. Those two stars are named Tle'dzot'ani (Starlight) and Tl'a'wet'ani (Fog Woman) and can still be seen in the night sky today.

In some versions of the story the woman is described as an old woman.

The two men heard a voice calling to them and they were afraid. They looked around but they could not see anyone. They heard the voice again and it said, "I am the Wind that blows on the waters and the waves are my voice. If you will give me your hearts, every time you hear the sound of the waves you will hear my voice and remember me." The two young men gave their hearts to the Wind and ever after, whenever they heard the sound of the waves they knew that the Wind was with them.

A large serpent came out of the water and took one of the young men. The other young man went back to the village and told the people what had happened. The chief of the village decided to go and get the man who had been taken by the serpent.
He took on the form of a killer whale and went to where the serpent had been. He arrived just in time to see the serpent swallowing the young man whole. The chief then took on the form of a large eagle and flew into the serpent's mouth. Inside the serpent's body, the chief changed back to his human form and fought the serpent from the inside. He killed the serpent and took its heart. The chief then returned to the village with the heart of the serpent.
The villagers celebrated the victory of their chief and made a feast in his honor. Since then, no one has been taken by the serpent in the story.
